thread_tweets.text: It's really an interesting question. If a public company pays the "fair market price" for a new business and the business was not part of a public company and they paid with cash (retained earnings).  The earnings grow the shares stay the same and there is zero reason the enterprise value should change so the stock price should stay the same and the multiple should fall.  Buying earnings growth that is useful to a company's stock price means buying the productive asset (a business or factory) building the asset themselves only accrues value if they buy/build the asset for less than fair value.  Got me thinking which is fun.

Here's my differentiation of the two ideas which may be wrong but it's my split

Return chasers are slow and late and literally pay the alpha to the momentum strategy who is earlier.

Any acquisition of a private company or a business of a private company with retained earnings (cash) grows earnings of the public company as well.  Does that mean the aggregate economy is seeing earnings growth?  No.  It's just showing up in public company earnings growth figures.

It's really an interesting question. If a public company pays the "fair market price" for a new business and the business was not part of a public company and they paid with cash (retained earnings).  The earnings grow the shares stay the same and there is zero reason the enterprise value should change so the stock price should stay the same and the multiple should fall.  Buying earnings growth that is useful to a company's stock price means buying the productive asset (a business or factory) building the asset themselves only accrues value if they buy/build the asset for less than fair value.  Got me thinking which is fun.

tweets.text:
Positioning tells you how crowded a trade is. The source of marginal demand could tell you how durable it may be.

Business activity can create recurring buying pressure that remains after sentiment cools. A durable supply sink can also support price by reducing the amount available to trade.

Momentum-driven positions behave differently. Rising prices attract more capital through a thin market, but that demand weakens when the rally stalls.

This is why co-movement says little about durability. Assets can sell off together without being supported in the same way.

The important question is where the support is after momentum turns.

We don’t have *autonomous* trading agents live yet (will have a beta for it soon).

To your point, our focus is to make it easy to backtest and paper-trade BEFORE you deploy capital.

So you increase the chance of having winning agents.

We want strong evidence that agents produced from our platform outperform retail investors before releasing.

If we don’t have that, we’re not releasing it.

BTW - some empirical data from our current “copilot” agentic experience:

Users who trade using our agent (in addition to manual trading) have a 66% higher chance of being profitable than those who only trade manually.

(Based on data collected in the last 9 months or so - may change going fwd.)

You can use this agent in our mobile app (Nansen AI) and on web today.
